panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: This is a sagittal whole-body CT from a 7-year-old patient with juvenile dermatomyositis. The arrows demonstrate extensive dystrophic calcification in the soft tissues and musculature, directly supporting the captioned diagnosis of calcinosis universalis. [raw subtype: jdm] B: This complementary sagittal CT view shows the same patient's extensive cervical, thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, and extremity soft-tissue and muscular calcifications. The finding is explicitly attributed by the caption to refractory juvenile dermatomyositis with calcinosis universalis. [raw subtype: jdm]

panels.figure_caption: Low-dose whole body CT of a 7-year-old female with refractory JDM and extensive calcinosis universalis. Arrows demonstrate prominent locations of the extensive calcifications in the soft tissues and musculature extending from the neck, along the torso, upper and lower extremities. Also demonstrated are intra-abdominal and pelvic calcifications
in_text_mentions: that is difficult to evaluate with one or two-dimensional X-ray images. CT can evaluate lesions that are not readily palpable on the skin, including lesions near internal organs and/or muscles (Fig. 2). CT has been used to image patients since the 1970s [24], with case reports of CT being used to describe calcinosis in dermatomyositis during the 1980s [25, 26]. These early reports highlight cases where CT of the thighs detected prominent calcinosis not previously identified on the skin [25, 26]. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: This is a real-patient abdominal radiograph from a child with juvenile dermatomyositis showing extensive radiographically apparent soft-tissue calcinosis. B: This is a real-patient left-knee radiograph from a child with juvenile dermatomyositis showing extensive soft-tissue and periarticular calcinosis. The visible 'L' laterality marker is an annotation.

X-ray became a modality to diagnose and monitor calcinosis as clinicians recognized the need to detect subcutaneous and intramuscular calcinosis, often missed on physical exam (Fig. 1) [11, 12]. In a retrospective study reviewing 29 JDM related calcinosis cases from 1950–1977, serial radiographs at 1–4-year intervals were able to follow the regression of the subcutaneous calcification in 8 out of 11 children and progression of calcinosis in one child [12].
